insight.title: GPS Satellites Have No Idea Where You Are
insight.subtitle: Your phone calculates its location entirely on its own by listening to atomic clocks in orbit.

sections.text: GPS satellites don’t track your phone. They are completely blind, broadcasting only their precise location and time. Millions of devices listen to this signal, but never send anything back to space.

Radio waves travel at light speed, so timestamps arrive slightly delayed. By comparing microscopic time differences from four satellites, your phone solves a simple geometric equation to pinpoint your exact location.
Because it’s a purely passive system, a mere thirty satellites can guide billions of cars, ships, and smartphones at the exact same second, perfectly immune to network congestion or server crashes.
Space broadcasts the time; your pocket solves the geometry.

audioBrief.script:
Welcome to your Sift Daily Briefing. Here is today's news made clear and simple.

The European Union and Indonesia signed a new bilateral trade agreement. The trade deal covers seven hundred thirty million people across both regions. It promises lower tariffs and new investment opportunities for both sides. The European Union signed the agreement to help diversify its global trade ties. This move comes amid growing economic tensions around the world.

Turning to technology news, the United States announced rules blocking Chinese firms from remotely using advanced chips. The Bureau of Industry and Security set an interim final rule for third-country data centers. Companies now need licenses to export advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil. Chinese firms previously accessed Nvidia chips through data centers in countries like Malaysia. This rule follows questions about Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and Megaspeed chief executive Alice Huang. China accused Washington of abusing export control measures to interfere in normal trade. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said China will act to protect its legitimate rights. President Donald Trump meets President Xi Jinping at a summit in Shenzhen in November twenty twenty-six.

In climate news, negotiators at the United Nations climate summit in Turkey went into overtime on Saturday. Work crews began packing up the venue in the coastal city of Antalya. The draft agreement faced strong criticism for failing to mention fossil fuels. One hundred civil society groups warned co-hosts Turkey and Australia about a disappointing outcome. The United Nations announced the world will likely pass the Paris goal of one point five degrees. Tuvalu Environment Minister Maina Talia said he is still trying to remain optimistic. The United States did not participate directly in this year's climate talks. The next UN climate summit will take place in Ethiopia in November twenty twenty-seven.

Next, European Union summit chairman Antonio Costa proposed new cuts to the seven-year budget draft. His proposal reduces the overall budget by forty billion euros to one point five eight two trillion. The cuts target industrial competitiveness, defense, and external spending. France criticized the numbers for not doing enough to protect farmers. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the proposed total budget figure is still too high. Costa also suggested a three percent digital tax on online advertising for large tech companies. This tax would mostly affect American technology companies like Google and Amazon. European Union leaders will discuss the proposal at a summit on November twenty-six.

In health news, a major medical study about Covid nineteen vaccines was retracted last month. The study from twenty twenty-two explored a vaccine design for broad virus immunity. The lead author in Britain admitted to fabricating data and falsifying images. International scientists had widely cited the research paper up until this year.

Moving to economic policy, President Donald Trump announced plans to tax American companies building data centers abroad. Trump stated at a White House briefing that overseas building allows China to take technology. The announcement came after he returned from a summit in China with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping. The president provided few details on how the government would enforce the new penalties. He also did not specify what legal authority allows him to carry out the plan. Some members of his own team heard about the policy for the first time.

Up next, President Trump discussed Jensen Huang with Xi Jinping as trade officials addressed Nvidia exports.

President Donald Trump said he discussed former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Nvidia is an American company that makes advanced artificial intelligence chips. Huang recently resigned following allegations of an affair with a Chinese spy. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Huang was not mentioned in his own separate talks with Chinese officials. Both statements were correct regarding their respective meetings, according to an anonymous senior official. Trump said he would like Huang to be restored as chief executive of Nvidia. Nvidia is not considering bringing Huang back, according to a person familiar with the matter. Bessent added that policy allowing sales of Nvidia H two hundred chips to China remains unchanged.

Turning to technology, quantum software companies are testing algorithms to manage energy grids and develop power materials. Quantum software uses specialized math to solve complex problems faster than traditional computers. Phasecraft is a quantum software firm founded in Bristol, England, in twenty nineteen. It raised thirty-four million dollars in twenty twenty-five and is opening offices in Arlington, Virginia. The company partnered with Britain's grid operator to manage power across England, Scotland, and Wales. Phasecraft says its software handles grid tasks up to one thousand times faster than traditional computers. Another firm, Quantinuum, is modeling materials for hydrogen fuel cells used in transportation. ORCA Computing partnered with energy company BP to study how biofuels burn.

Next, President Donald Trump said he would work with Democrats to cap credit card rates at ten percent. The median credit card interest rate is about twenty-two point two percent, according to federal data. Banks said an interest rate cap would force them to cancel cards for less creditworthy customers. Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren expressed support for capping credit card interest rates. Republican Senator Josh Hawley has also introduced a bill to cap credit card rates. Capping rates at ten percent would save Americans roughly one hundred billion dollars annually, according to researchers. Americans carry about one point two three trillion dollars in credit card debt, according to federal figures.

In international news, a Russian cargo ship caught fire in the Baltic Sea following a drone attack. Finland said Ukraine was likely responsible for hitting the vessel. The ship, named Sparta Two, was damaged in international waters before drifting into Finnish territory. All sixteen crew members evacuated onto lifeboats and transferred to a nearby Russian ship. The cargo vessel is owned by a shipping company that provides logistics for the Russian Defence Ministry. Finland introduced temporary maritime restrictions in the Gulf of Finland to protect civilians. The ship remains anchored in Finnish waters while local authorities lead rescue operations. Separately, a Russian governor said eighty drones were shot down over the Leningrad region overnight.

Moving to politics, thirteen new Black Democratic lawmakers will join the United States Congress in January. This represents the largest new cohort of Black Democratic members since nineteen ninety-three. Four of the new members are thirty-four years old or younger. Black candidates won fifty-eight seats in the House of Representatives during the recent midterm elections. Black representation in the Senate reached a record seven members following two Democratic election victories. Four Black Republicans are leaving Congress, leaving Senator Tim Scott as the sole Black Republican lawmaker. Two additional Black Democratic candidates in Louisiana will compete in runoff elections on December twelfth. Congressional Black Caucus chair Yvette Clarke said affordability is the primary concern for constituents.

Finally, proposed legislation in Kenya would require internet providers to track data usage and issue metered bills. Lawmaker Marianne Jebet Kitany sponsored the bill to ensure consumers pay only for data they use. The bill requires providers to assign each customer a unique meter number and submit annual billing reports. Telecommunications companies and civil society groups warned that mandatory metering could harm subscriber privacy and raise costs. The Communications Authority of Kenya urged lawmakers not to make metered billing compulsory. Separately, student David Ooga Mokaya won court protection preventing officials from sharing his private phone data without consent. The parliamentary committee on communication is currently reviewing the proposed internet metering legislation.

Before we go, here is your thought for the day.

GPS satellites orbiting Earth do not actually track your smartphone. The satellites are completely blind and only broadcast their exact location and time. Millions of everyday devices listen to these radio signals, but send nothing back into space. Radio waves travel at light speed, meaning timestamps arrive with tiny delays. Your phone compares microscopic time differences from four satellites to solve a geometric equation. That simple math calculation pinpoints your exact location. Because it is a passive system, just thirty satellites can guide billions of users at once. It never suffers from network congestion or server crashes. It is fascinating how space broadcasts time while your pocket calculates where you are. Next time you open a map, will you notice the invisible math guiding your steps?

Thank you for listening to the Sift Daily Briefing, and stay curious until next time.

audioBriefIndepth.script:
Welcome to your Sift In-Depth Briefing. This show brings you full analysis on the stories shaping our world today.

The European Union and Indonesia have signed a bilateral trade agreement. This deal covers seven hundred thirty million people. It promises lower tariffs and new investment opportunities across both regions. The agreement comes as the European Union works to broaden its global trade ties. European officials hope to diversify partnerships amid growing global economic tensions.

Now we turn to a developing story about technology, power, and international business.

Can a government stop another country from renting high-tech equipment over the internet? The United States introduced strict export rules to block Chinese companies from accessing advanced AI chips remotely.

Computer chips power artificial intelligence, which helps software analyze data and solve complex problems. The United States designs the world's most advanced AI chips through companies like Nvidia. To protect national security, Washington banned direct sales of advanced semiconductors to China. However, companies soon found simple ways around those trade restrictions. Chinese firms could not buy the physical chips for their own computers. Instead, they rented computing power over the internet from foreign data centres in nearby countries. Nvidia founder Jensen Huang built a strong business supplying chips to those overseas facilities. He also publicly argued that China should have access to advanced AI technology.

The situation changed when personal and security scandals involving Huang came to light. United States authorities discovered that a Singapore data company named Megaspeed had ties to an alleged spy. Megaspeed was a key buyer of Nvidia chips in Southeast Asia. Huang had also failed to disclose personal relationships with employees, creating serious conflicts of interest. Nvidia removed Huang from his post, which caused company shares to fall sharply.

In response, the United States Commerce Department announced an interim final rule to stop remote access arrangements. The Bureau of Industry and Security added new license requirements for shipping chips to five countries. Those nations are Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. American officials said those places carry a higher risk of technology diversion to China. Beijing strongly criticized the move, calling it economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Washington is abusing export control measures. China's Ministry of Commerce warned that the rule disrupts the global semiconductor supply chain. China stated the American action violates the common understanding previously reached between both heads of state. Meanwhile, Nvidia stock sank twenty-two point nine percent last week alone. Nvidia reported strong third-quarter financial numbers despite the drop in its stock price. The shares have fallen thirty-eight point seven percent since late last month. The S and P five hundred index fell eight point eight percent during that same time frame. The Nasdaq one hundred index dropped eleven point eight percent as well.

Washington issued this rule right before President Donald Trump travels to Shenzhen for diplomatic talks. He plans to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the APEC summit. American officials wanted to strengthen trade enforcement before those leaders sat down together.

This restriction cuts off remote computing options for Chinese artificial intelligence developers. The shift has sparked broader debates about how to regulate powerful tech companies. For example, AI developer Anthropic is using multiple share classes to give independent trustees oversight. Anthropic reached a valuation of one point five trillion dollars within six years of its founding. Observers are now watching whether China will enact specific trade countermeasures against American businesses.

In another part of the world, international negotiators are struggling to reach a consensus.

Why are diplomats staying extra days at the annual United Nations climate summit? Negotiators extended their talks into overtime because countries could not agree on fossil fuels and climate funding.

Every year, representatives from nearly two hundred countries gather at global climate summits. These annual meetings help nations cut carbon emissions and adapt to rising temperatures. In twenty fifteen, world leaders signed the landmark Paris Agreement. They set a target to limit global warming to one point five degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Burning coal, oil, and gas releases greenhouse gases that trap solar heat. That trapped heat causes record heat waves, destructive floods, and rising sea levels. Developing nations suffer heavy impacts despite creating very little historical pollution. Small island countries face deep risks as rising ocean waters wash over their shorelines. These vulnerable nations want wealthy countries to provide financial assistance for climate recovery. However, oil and gas producing nations regularly push back against strict limits on fossil fuels.

Tensions peaked when summit leaders published a draft agreement on Thursday. The draft document completely removed earlier references to ending fossil fuel use. It also deleted a proposed one hundred twenty billion dollar target for adaptation funding. Observers noted that Saudi Arabia and other energy producers opposed that draft language.

The summit in Antalya, Turkey, went into overtime as negotiations stretched past Friday. Venue workers boxed up electronics and took down displays in empty hallways. ActionAid International climate lead Teresa Anderson noted that no one knows what is happening behind closed doors. European Union Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra stated there will be a good deal or no deal. Turkey's COP31 President Murat Kurum asked delegates to act responsibly and avoid getting hung up on words. A letter from one hundred civil society groups warned this could become a historical low point. During a Friday session, a protester clambered onto a table to denounce the missing fossil fuel text. The United States did not participate directly in the summit for the second year in a row. President Donald Trump previously stopped American cooperation on climate policy, calling global warming a hoax.

Talks hit a crisis point because recent data shows global warming is worsening fast. A U.N. report recently warned the world will likely overshoot the one point five degree warming threshold. Gambia negotiator Isatou Camara suggested some nations use delays to force tired delegates into weaker deals.

Without an agreement on fossil fuels, efforts to combat climate change remain stalled for another year. The current draft calls for carbon removal technologies to lower temperatures after an overshoot occurs. However, Malawi negotiator Brenda Mwale questioned whether the conference suffered from a leadership crisis. The next climate summit will take place in Ethiopia's capital, Addis Ababa, in November twenty twenty-seven. Negotiators will now attempt to draft a fresh text before delegates return home.

Next, the chair of European Union leaders proposes cuts to the EU budget draft and suggests a digital tax.

How will European Union leaders fund their shared priorities over the next seven years? Antonio Costa proposed cutting the draft budget while creating a new digital tax on global tech giants.

The European Union plans its spending in seven-year budgets. This shared fund supports farmers, builds new technology, and helps poorer regions raise their living standards. It also pays for student exchanges, aid to Ukraine, and official salaries. Member countries pay into the budget based on their economic size. The budget also receives direct money from customs duties, value-added taxes, and plastic waste fees. Countries that pay more than they receive are called net contributors. Net beneficiaries get more funding back than they pay in. Over recent years, high energy prices and increased defense spending pushed national budgets hard. Germany, the largest net contributor, repeatedly called for shrinking the total spending package by hundreds of billions of euros. Meanwhile, smaller countries fought to protect funding for their local regions and agriculture.

To bridge these differences, Costa offered a new compromise plan. His proposal cuts the overall draft budget by forty billion euros. That brings the seven-year total down to one point five eight two trillion euros.

Costa’s draft makes its biggest cuts to defense, foreign aid, and the European Competitiveness Fund. That fund helps European industries compete against rivals in China and the United States. Funding for agriculture and regional development received relatively more protection under this draft. However, France criticized the numbers for not protecting farmers enough. Siegfried Muresan, the chief budget negotiator for the European Parliament, rejected the proposal completely. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called the cuts a good first step, but said the total remains too high. Merz also insisted that all twenty-seven countries must share the budget burden fairly. To raise fresh revenue, Costa suggested a three percent tax on large digital companies like Google, Apple, and Meta. He also proposed slowing down capital repayments for the post-pandemic recovery fund.

Leaders want to resolve this battle quickly. Seven member nations face national elections next year, where budget fights could stir up political trouble.

EU leaders will discuss Costa’s proposal at a special summit on November twenty-sixth and twenty-seventh. All twenty-seven nations must agree unanimously before the budget can take effect.

In medical news, a major study on coronavirus vaccines was pulled after researchers discovered fabricated data. The twenty-twenty-two study explored a vaccine design meant to protect against multiple virus mutations. Its lead author admitted to falsifying images and fabricating data in the paper. Scientists widely cited the paper until last month, when the journal officially retracted the work.

Turning to technology and security, why is Washington struggling to protect its digital networks while building advanced software? President Donald Trump replaced his top cybersecurity official after rapid software updates caused a series of system outages.

The United States leads the world in building artificial intelligence hardware and cloud storage. American companies like Nvidia, Google, and Amazon design almost all advanced data-center chips. At the same time, cyber defense is changing fast. AI models like Anthropic's Mythos preview scan computer systems to spot security bugs automatically. Companies use these tools to find flaws quickly before malicious hackers can exploit them. To fix those flaws, engineers release software patches. However, pushing out fast updates carries a known risk. Stacking up multiple quick patches can accidentally crash complex computer networks.

That digital fragility became clear when rapid patching triggered unexpected system outages across major organizations. Brief disruptions hit Microsoft email, Federal Aviation Administration flight systems, JPMorgan Chase banking services, and internal communication networks at the National Security Agency.

Following those disruptions, President Trump removed Sean Cairncross from his post as National Cyber Director. Trump stated publicly that Cairncross was not doing a good job. The president then appointed Kirsten Davies to take over top cybersecurity duties. Meanwhile, American officials are facing broader worries about AI infrastructure. The Commerce Department recently closed a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to access foreign AI chips remotely. Yet American-owned data centers abroad still rent capacity to services running Chinese AI models, including DeepSeek and Kimi K3.

These security decisions come as AI tools speed up both cyber defenses and cyber attacks. Software frameworks now let automated tools scan targets constantly without stopping.

Officials will watch how Davies handles network stability as security threats expand. Meanwhile, experts suggest Washington may promote American open-source AI models to keep US infrastructure serving domestic tools.

Next, we turn to reports that President Trump discussed Nvidia chief Jensen Huang with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Are United States rules on selling advanced computer chips to China about to change? Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says existing policy allowing sales of older chips remains in place.

American firms lead the world in making chips for artificial intelligence, which powers smart software. Government leaders worry these chips could help foreign militaries grow stronger. Because of these security risks, the United States places strict limits on selling them overseas. Nvidia became the dominant maker of these specialized computer chips. Its founder and chief executive officer was Jensen Huang. Huang resigned recently after reports of an affair with a Singapore business executive. United States intelligence agencies suspect that executive was a spy for China. Her company, Megaspeed, let Chinese businesses use Nvidia chips remotely to run complex programs. Colette Kress took over as interim leader after Huang left the company.

President Donald Trump traveled to Shenzhen, China, for a historic summit with leader Xi Jinping. After the trip, top officials publicly addressed chip export rules and Huang's future.

President Trump said he spoke with Xi about Huang and called Huang a brilliant man. Trump stated he would love to see Huang get a second chance as chief executive. A person familiar with the matter said Nvidia is not considering bringing Huang back. A congressional report revealed the Commerce Department approved eight hundred seventy-nine thousand eight hundred sixty-eight chips. Companies requested over three point four million chips across twenty-one applications. Approved shipments included seventy-five thousand chips for Alibaba and one hundred fifty thousand for Tencent. They also included forty-three thousand for Baidu and four thousand for BYD. The Defense Department says each of those four companies has ties to China's military. Nvidia said its shipments were fully legal, but confirmed it has now stopped H two hundred sales. Rival chipmaker AMD also stated that it complies with all export regulations. Bessent had previously criticized Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for delaying strict export controls. But Bessent now says proper restrictions are in place and remote access is blocked. Trump defended Lutnick, calling him a different kind of guy with strong business instincts.

These updates happen now because administration leaders had been arguing over how strictly to enforce chip limits.

This signals that the White House may focus on remote access rather than tighter sales bans. Chinese tech firms may face slower progress as access to top hardware remains restricted. Listeners can watch whether Congress pushes for stricter bans on future chip license applications.

While chipmakers navigate global trade rules, another branch of computing is aiming to solve real-world energy problems.

Where will quantum computers make their first big impact on our daily lives? New quantum software is tackling practical energy challenges instead of long-term medical research.

Quantum computers process information using physics rules that normal computers cannot match. For years, scientists promised quantum machines would quickly create new life-saving drugs. They also promised to fix complex global shipping routes and airline schedules. However, building quantum hardware powerful enough for medical research remains decades away. Instead, software developers began writing algorithms for existing, smaller quantum devices. Algorithms are set instructions that tell a computer how to solve specific mathematical problems. These algorithms can model how tiny physical particles interact with each other in nature. Researchers realized this skill is perfect for testing materials used in power systems.

Quantum software start-ups began shifting focus toward immediate opportunities in the energy sector. Companies are now securing millions in funding to deploy these specialized programs today.

British company Phasecraft announced expansion plans to set up American headquarters in Arlington, Virginia. Phasecraft raised thirty-four million dollars in funding in twenty twenty-five to build energy software. Chief executive officer Ashley Montanaro stated that improving energy systems offers real commercial returns. Phasecraft works with the National Energy System Operator to manage electrical grids in Britain. It claims its software solves grid emergency tasks up to one thousand times faster than standard computers. Phasecraft also partnered with Oxford PV to design more efficient solar cell materials. Another project uses Boston-based QuEra hardware and Harvard University research under government agency ARPA-E. That project aims to replace scarce iridium metal used in hydrogen fuel production. Rival firm Quantinuum models materials for transportation fuel cells and carbon capture projects. Spinout ORCA Computing partnered with BP and Britain's National Quantum Computing Centre on power grid scheduling.

This push is happening now because expanding renewable power makes electric grids harder to balance. Power operators need instant answers to prevent blackouts when solar or wind energy fluctuates.

Faster energy calculations could lower operating costs and reduce strain on existing power lines. It may also speed up the creation of cheaper clean energy technologies. Listeners can watch to see if power grid operators in Asia adopt these quantum programs next.

While high-tech computing tries to lower energy bills, lawmakers are turning their attention to household debt.

Could there soon be a strict legal limit on credit card interest rates? President Donald Trump plans to join incoming Congressional Democrats to cap credit card interest at ten percent.

Americans carry more credit card debt than ever before, reaching one point two three trillion dollars. In twenty twenty-four, about one hundred ninety-five million Americans paid one hundred sixty billion dollars in interest. The New York Federal Reserve reported that the median credit card interest rate reached twenty-two point two percent. During his campaign, President Trump promised to cap those interest rates to help struggling households. He formally proposed the ten percent limit in January as part of an affordability plan. Banks and credit card companies strongly fought the idea from the start. Lenders warned a cap would force them to cancel cards for lower-income borrowers. They also warned that popular card rewards and cash-back perks would be severely cut back. Republicans in Congress showed little interest in pushing the bill forward, so the plan stalled.

Control of Congress shifted to Democrats, creating a new political path for the proposed rate cap.

Speaking to Fox News, President Trump said he would work with Democrats to pass the cap. Trump argued that credit card companies have made a lot of money off consumers. Democrat Elizabeth Warren welcomed the move, saying Congress should pass the cap to save Americans money. Warren is expected to chair the Senate Banking Committee in the incoming Congress. Representative Maxine Waters and Republican Senator Josh Hawley have also supported capping rates. Under a ten percent cap, a five thousand dollar balance costs forty-two dollars monthly in interest. At current average rates, that same balance costs about one hundred dollars each month. Researchers estimate a ten percent limit would save Americans roughly one hundred billion dollars a year. Those same researchers note credit card companies would remain profitable despite losing revenue.

This effort is gaining momentum now because both parties face intense public pressure to deliver economic relief.

If passed, millions of borrowers could see significant savings on their monthly card statements. However, consumers might lose rewards points or find it harder to get approved for new credit. Listeners can watch whether bipartisan legislation moves quickly through the Senate Banking Committee next year.

Up next, a dashcam captures a Russian missile strike on Lviv, Ukraine.

Why did a Russian cargo ship catch fire in the Baltic Sea? A drone strike hit the vessel, forcing its crew to abandon ship.

To understand this event, we must look at how the war in Europe spread. In twenty twenty-two, Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Ukraine began fighting back to defend its land and its people. As fighting continued, nearby countries grew deeply concerned about their safety. Finland and Sweden decided to change their historical defense policies. Finland joined the NATO military alliance in twenty twenty-three. Sweden joined the NATO alliance in twenty twenty-four. NATO is a group of nations that promise to defend one another. The Gulf of Finland is a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea between Finland and Estonia. Recently, Ukraine has sent waves of military drones toward Russia's Leningrad region. Some drones strayed into airspace near NATO territory. That raised fears that war could affect nearby European nations.

On November twenty-first, a Russian cargo ship called the Sparta II was sailing in the Baltic Sea. Shipping data from LSEG shows the ship left St Petersburg on November twentieth. It was heading to Kaliningrad, a Russian area between Poland and Lithuania. The United States has placed sanctions on this vessel. The ship is linked to a logistics company called Oboronlogistika. That company provides logistics services for the Russian Defence Ministry. Border Guard Commander Ilja Iljin said the ship might carry military materiel. Two drones struck the one hundred twenty-one meter vessel near Gogland island. The strike started a fire on board the ship. The sixteen crew members evacuated onto lifeboats and then moved to a nearby Russian vessel. The burning ship drifted into Finnish waters and dropped anchor. Finnish authorities then took control of the rescue effort.

Finland said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Armed forces spokesperson Aki-Mauri Huhtinen said it was unclear why the ship was targeted. Swedish Defence Minister Pal Jonson said Swedish combat aircraft flew under Finnish command. Estonia sent a navy vessel to help fight fires and handle potential pollution. Finnish Coast Guard Commander Mikko Simola said a Russian helicopter was suspected of briefly violating Finnish airspace. Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said the war is spilling over into neighboring areas. Estonia's Prime Minister Kristen Michal said this shows the consequences of fighting Russia's aggression. Helsinki set temporary air and sea rules in the eastern Gulf of Finland to protect civilians. Neither Ukraine's Foreign Ministry nor Russia's embassy in Helsinki immediately responded to requests for comment.

This incident happened now because Ukraine is expanding drone strikes against Russian logistics routes. Leningrad governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said eighty drones were shot down overnight in his region. Finland's military also detected a strike on a Russian warship nearby last week. This event shows that naval routes near NATO countries are becoming part of the war zone. Kaliningrad governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said the strike creates no supply threat for his region. In the coming days, observers can watch whether Russian ships tow the Sparta II back home.

Moving across the ocean, another major political shift is taking shape in the United States.

How will a new generation of Black lawmakers change the United States Congress? A record number of new Black Democrats will take office this January after recent elections.

To understand this moment, we must look back at how representation grew in Washington. For decades, Black leaders fought to win equal political power in American government. In nineteen ninety-three, sixteen first-time Black members entered Congress together. That historic wave helped many members build long careers and gain power on key committees. Five of the six longest-serving Black House members were first elected in nineteen ninety-one or nineteen ninety-three. Dedrick Asante-Muhammad of the Joint Center for Political and Economic Studies said earlier waves pay off decades later. Over time, those leaders created the Congressional Black Caucus to push for civil rights and economic policies. Professor Andra Gillespie of Emory University noted proportional representation allows diverse voices across congressional committees.

In April, the Supreme Court issued a ruling that weakened the Voting Rights Act of nineteen sixty-five. After that ruling, Republican state legislatures redrew voting maps in several states. Four districts held by Black Democrats were affected by those redrawn political maps. Representative Shomari Figures of Alabama and Don Davis of North Carolina both won reelection anyway. Voters overall elected thirteen new Black Democrats to the House of Representatives.

This is the largest new class of Black Democratic members joining Congress since nineteen ninety-three. Four of these new members are thirty-four years old or younger. Melat Kiros, who is twenty-nine, is the first female Gen Z member elected to Congress. She is also the first Black woman elected to represent Colorado. Other young members include Darializa Avila Chevalier, Adrian Boafo, and Donavan McKinney. In contrast, senior Black leaders include Representative Maxine Waters, eighty-eight, and Bennie Thompson, seventy-eight. Reelected Pennsylvania Democrat Summer Lee described herself as unapologetically progressive and called for bold leadership.

In the Senate, representation reached a record seven Black members. Juliana Stratton won in Illinois, while Scott Colom won an upset victory in Mississippi. Colom will be Mississippi's first Black senator in more than one hundred forty years. Georgia Senator Raphael Warnock campaigned for Colom and emphasized reducing healthcare costs and ending tariffs. Overall, Black candidates won fifty-eight seats in the four hundred thirty-five member House. Two additional seats in Louisiana will be decided in December twelfth runoffs. Four Black Republicans are leaving Congress, leaving Senator Tim Scott as the only Black Republican remaining. The Congressional Black Caucus will enter the next session with a record sixty-four members. Chair Yvette Clarke said members feel urgent pressure to address community crises, especially affordability. Representative Hakeem Jeffries is the favorite to become House speaker and lead the Democratic caucus. Political science professor Periloux Peay noted leadership must handle strong pressure from progressive members.

This shift is happening now as November midterm elections bring a younger generation into leadership. This new group could shape policy on voting rights, healthcare costs, and economic rules. Major laws will still require bipartisan support in the Senate and could face vetoes by President Donald Trump. Next month, observers can watch the December twelfth runoffs in Louisiana to see the final caucus size.

Turning now to international technology news, a new proposal is sparking debate over internet rules in Africa.

Why is a new internet proposal causing widespread worry in Kenya? A proposed law would require internet providers to track data usage with individual meter numbers.

To understand this debate, we must look at how digital services operate across Kenya. In recent years, internet access has grown rapidly for schools, businesses, and everyday communication. Most mobile phone users already pay for the exact volume of data they consume. However, fixed home and business broadband connections usually offer unlimited access for a fixed monthly rate. In twenty nineteen, Kenya passed the Data Protection Act to safeguard personal information. Even with that law, questions about how authorities access telecom records have reached local courts. In November twenty twenty-four, student David Ooga Mokaya was arrested over a social media post. Senior Principal Magistrate Caroline Nyaguthii acquitted Mokaya after prosecutors failed to prove the charges. Mokaya then filed a High Court petition arguing police obtained his location and call data without consent. In February, Justice Bahati Mwamuye issued interim orders restricting any disclosure of Mokaya's data.

Now, Kenya's parliament is considering the Kenya Information and Communications Amendment Bill of twenty twenty-five. Sponsored by Aldai Member of Parliament Marianne Jebet Kitany, the bill mandates consumption-based internet billing. Under the bill, internet service providers must assign every customer a unique meter number to track data. Providers would convert consumption into readable details and send billing data to the regulator each financial year. The bill's goal is to protect consumers so they pay only for the internet they use. However, Demas Kiprono of ICJ Kenya argued the regulator already possesses adequate powers to resolve billing disputes.

The National Assembly's Departmental Committee on Communication, Information and Innovation is currently reviewing the proposal. On November tenth, Telkom Kenya Chief Executive Officer Mugo Kibati testified before the parliamentary committee. Kibati explained that mobile internet accounts for ninety-six percent of data subscriptions and is already volume-billed. The law would mainly impact fixed broadband, which represents the remaining four percent of subscriptions. Kibati warned that mandatory metering could increase compliance costs and harm future investment in broadband networks. Instead, Telkom proposed that companies clearly disclose billing models and fair-use policies before customers subscribe.

On November third, the Communications Authority of Kenya also urged lawmakers not to make metering compulsory. The regulator warned that forced metering could increase costs for students, low-income households, and small businesses. Background software updates, cloud services, and streaming can consume data without subscribers noticing. The regulator suggested alternative measures like usage alerts at fifty, eighty, and one hundred percent of data limits. It also recommended free real-time usage dashboards, spending caps, and regular independent audits of billing systems.

This debate is happening right now because parliament is actively drafting the final text of the bill. If passed, mandatory metering could increase costs for heavy internet users and raise new data privacy questions. In the coming weeks, observers can watch whether lawmakers adopt the regulator's voluntary guidelines instead.

Before we go, here is your thought for the day.

Many people assume that GPS satellites high above Earth are constantly watching and tracking our movements. In reality, GPS satellites have no idea where you are. They are completely blind. The satellites do not watch us at all. Instead, they simply broadcast their own precise location and the exact time. Millions of everyday devices listen to this continuous signal. However, your phone never sends any message back into space. Radio waves travel at the speed of light. Because of that speed, timestamps from space arrive at your device with microscopic delays. Your phone picks up those radio signals and measures the tiny time differences. By comparing signals from four satellites, your phone solves a simple geometric equation. That single calculation allows your phone to pinpoint your exact location entirely on its own. This design is genuinely interesting because the entire network functions as a purely passive system. Space simply broadcasts the time, and the device in your pocket solves the geometry. Because phones only listen, a mere thirty satellites can guide billions of cars, ships, and smartphones. They guide all of those devices at the exact same second. The system is perfectly immune to network congestion or server crashes. It never slows down, even when millions of people check their location at once. It is remarkable how much we rely on atomic clocks quietly orbiting in space. The next time you check your map, will you remember the atomic clocks ticking in orbit?

Thank you for spending this time with Sift In-Depth. Take care, and we will talk again soon.

audioBriefCalm.script:
Welcome to your Sift Daily Briefing. Here is the clear, plain version of today's news.

First, the European Union and Indonesia signed a bilateral trade agreement. This new economic deal covers seven hundred thirty million people. The agreement promises lower tariffs and new investment opportunities. The European Union wants to diversify its trade ties. It is doing this amid growing global economic tensions.

In international trade, the United States announced rules curbing Chinese firms from remotely accessing advanced artificial intelligence chips. The rule applies to data centres in third-party countries. On November seventeenth, twenty twenty-six, China accused Washington of abusing export control measures. The move follows scrutiny over chipmaker Nvidia and its sales to data centres in Southeast Asia. The Commerce Department now requires licenses for semiconductor transfers to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. The rule came before President Donald Trump met with President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun called the move economic coercion. China said it will do what is necessary to safeguard its legitimate rights.

Turning to climate news, global climate talks in Antalya, Turkey went into overtime on Saturday. Negotiators met to seek an agreement on handling worsening global warming. Critics condemned a draft deal for failing to mention fossil fuels. One hundred civil society groups sent a letter warning the summit could become a major disappointment. The United Nations announced the world will likely blow past its limit of one point five degrees Celsius. Tuvalu Environment Minister Maina Talia called for wealthy nations to contribute more disaster recovery funds. The United States did not participate directly in this year's climate summit. The next summit will take place in Ethiopia in November twenty twenty-seven.

In European news, summit chairman Antonio Costa proposed new cuts to the European Union budget draft. His proposal lowers the seven-year budget by forty billion euros to one point five eight two trillion euros. The plan reduces spending on competitiveness, defence, and external funding. Costa also suggested a three percent digital tax on major technology companies to create new revenue. European Parliament chief negotiator Siegfried Muresan called the proposed cuts unacceptable. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the proposed overall budget total was still too high. Four countries, including Hungary and Slovakia, do not want to fund aid for Ukraine. Leaders will discuss these proposals at a special summit on November twenty-sixth.

Now to medical news, a major coronavirus vaccine study was retracted last month after data fabrication was uncovered. The twenty twenty-two study explored a design for broad vaccine immunity. Its lead author, then based in Britain, admitted to fabricating data and falsifying images in the paper. International scientists had widely cited the study up until this year.

Turning to technology news, President Donald Trump announced plans to penalise American companies building data centers abroad. Speaking at a White House briefing, he stated China would take all of those facilities otherwise. He said he plans to impose a tremendous tax and heavy penalties on those companies. Trump made the statement after returning from a summit in China with President Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. During the briefing, the president offered little clarity regarding the war with Iran. Trump provided few details on the specific legal authority available to carry out his proposal. Some members of his own team were hearing about the potential policy for the first time.

Next, President Trump says he discussed Nvidia leader Jensen Huang with President Xi Jinping.

President Donald Trump said he discussed former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Huang was not mentioned in his separate talks with Chinese officials. A senior official said both statements were correct regarding their own separate conversations. Trump said he would like to see Huang returned as chief executive of Nvidia. Huang had resigned amid allegations of an affair with a Chinese spy. Nvidia is the U.S. company that makes powerful artificial intelligence chips. Bessent said U.S. policy allowing sales of Nvidia H200 chips to China continues as planned. Trump met with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China, this week.

Turning to technology, quantum software is being tested to help solve real-world energy challenges. Phasecraft is a quantum software firm founded in Bristol, England, in twenty nineteen. The company raised thirty-four million dollars in funding in twenty twenty-five. It plans to open U.S. headquarters in Arlington, Virginia. Phasecraft partners with grid operators to manage power exchanges during emergencies. The company says its software acts up to one thousand times faster than normal computers. It also works with Oxford PV to design efficient solar cells. Quantinuum uses quantum tools to design hydrogen fuel cells for transportation. ORCA Computing partnered with BP to study how biofuels burn.

In national policy, President Donald Trump promised to work with Democrats on capping credit card interest rates. The proposed plan would limit credit card interest rates to ten percent. The median credit card interest rate is roughly twenty-two point two percent, according to Federal Reserve data. Trump first proposed the ten percent limit in January to lower living costs. Banks opposed the cap, saying it could force them to cancel cards for poorer customers. Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren endorsed the cap to save Americans money. Researchers say a ten percent cap would save Americans about one hundred billion dollars each year. Americans currently carry about one point two three trillion dollars in total credit card debt.

Looking at Congress, thirteen new Black Democratic lawmakers will join the House of Representatives in January. This represents the largest new group of Black Democratic lawmakers since nineteen ninety-three. Four of the incoming lawmakers are thirty-four years old or younger. Black candidates won fifty-eight seats in the House during November's midterm elections. Two additional seats in Louisiana will be decided in runoff elections on December twelfth. Democrat Juliana Stratton won a Senate seat in Illinois. Democrat Scott Colom won an upset Senate election in Mississippi. Total Black representation in the United States Senate reached a record high of seven members. Representative Yvette Clarke said caucus members want bold action on the affordability crisis.

In world news, a proposed law in Kenya would make metered internet billing mandatory for users. Lawmaker Marianne Jebet Kitany sponsored the twenty twenty-five bill to prevent unfair internet billing. The law would force internet providers to assign every customer a unique meter number. Companies would monitor data usage and issue invoices based on exact consumption. The Communications Authority of Kenya urged lawmakers not to make metered billing compulsory. Telecom firm Telkom Kenya warned the system could harm user privacy and affordability. Civil society groups questioned how personal usage records would be collected and shared. Opponents say lawmakers must clarify how existing data protection laws would apply. A parliamentary committee is currently reviewing the proposed legislation.

Before we go, here is your thought for the day.

GPS satellites in orbit never actually track where your smartphone is located. The satellites are completely blind, broadcasting only their exact time and position. Millions of devices listen to this signal, but never send any data back to space. Radio waves travel at light speed, so timestamps arrive with microscopic time delays. By comparing timing differences from four satellites, your phone solves a simple geometric equation. This passive system allows just thirty satellites to guide billions of cars, ships, and phones. Because your phone only listens, the network never suffers from server crashes or congestion. Space constantly broadcasts the time, while the device in your pocket solves the geometry. How would our daily travel change if these space clocks suddenly stopped broadcasting?

Thank you for tuning in to today's edition of the Sift Daily Briefing.
